speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, November 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) that Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act, be read the third time and passed.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, let me start by congratulating the Minister of National Health and Welfare on his bill. Certainly it is never too late. One would suggest we should have seen the problem with our pension plans that we are trying to deal with in the bill today. We should have seen that a while back. Unfortunately through a miscalculation it was not the case.
The bill in fact was introduced in order to ensure the future viability of the Canada Pension Plan. I think in my view that is the thrust of the bill. Along with that there are a number of accessories that come with it such as the proposal to increase the Canada Pension Plan benefit for dependant children of disabled and deceased contributors by approximately 30 per cent. This means that if you want to look at it in terms of dollars and cents that will increase the benefit from about $113 to approximately $148 a month.
As a result of that there are close to 170,000 children across Canada who would receive those benefits at an approximate cost of $75 million to the government.
There are also some other changes that were introduced as a part of the bill. In a way there were some minor amendments such as amending the legislation to protect the benefit eligibility of Canada Pension Plan benefit contributors who are unable to apply in time because of incapacity. Also it extends benefits to children who come under the custody or control of an individual who is already receiving disability benefits.
This is more or less the main structure of what we are dealing with today. Under the new legislation, in order to adjust the misfortune, what we are going to see is the combined employee-employer contribution rate increasing gradually in steps starting in 1991. It will go from 4.6 per cent and will move up until the year 2011 where we will see approximately a 9.1 per cent increase. Compare that to what we have presently. If we were not increasing those contributions, then by the year 2011 an employee and an employer would only contribute about 7.6 per cent.
This is as a result of the fact that department officials or those who were involved with the calculation made the assumption that the birth rate in Canada in the 1970s was going to be at a certain level. Unfortunately those forecasts and figures were not accurate. At that time it was estimated there would be sue workers that would be available to provide benefits for each retired worker in the future. But because of the decline in the birth rate we are seeing now that there are only three workers in

Government Orders
the work force who would be paying benefits for a retired individual.
As a result of that there is a tremendous shortfall in terms of the pension plan. In the year 2011 or 2016 we are going to see quite a bit of difficulty.
Before I move on I want to congratulate our critic for National Health and Welfare, the member for Winnipeg North. He made an excellent presentation yesterday and attempted to introduce some amendments to the legislation. Unfortunately most of those amendments were not accepted by the government. It is too bad because most of those amendments were excellent ones. I would suggest that the government should look at them again and see if it could change its view and its mind. It could hopefully approach the Senate in order to reintroduce them and deal with them.
When we talk about pensions the first thing that comes to my mind is those who receive the pension benefit and those who are no longer in the work force, our senior citizen population.
As you know by the year 2031 the proportion of the population aged 65 years and over will increase approximately four times. If you recall in 1971 we had approximately 8 per cent of population at age 65 years of age and over. According to Statistics Canada, in the year 2031 we will have in excess of eight million Canadians who will be eligible to collect pensions and who are senior citizens. That will be out of a total population of about 32 million people.
In the short term the proportion of seniors is expected to rise about 15.7 per cent by the year 2011. That will translate to approximately five million senior citizens. So it can be seen why the government is moving with its proposal now in order to avoid difficulties at a later date.
Not only are we faced with an aging population in the year 2011 and beyond, but we are also faced with a shrinkage in terms of the tax base. We will not have enough people in the work force in order to support all the existing programs or all the possible programs we might be thinking of in the future unless something drastic is to take place.
That is why I have been speaking over the past two and a half years about the importance of putting a lot more emphasis on education, investing in research and development, combating illiteracy and training and retraining our work force. It seems like every time I look at a piece of legislation or a bill before this House, if there is a deficiency or a better way to do it, the answer always seems to be that it may be through education and investment in the future of Canadians.
You will be interested to know that our population is not only aging but thanks to the technical talents of people in the industry they are even living longer. For instance in the period from 1966 to 1986, the number of men over the age of 90 has doubled while the number of women over the age of 90 has tripled.
It is also startling that as people get older they are moving away from their families. For example in 1986 about 86 per cent of men between the ages of 55 and 64 lived in a family home. For men over 75 the percentage was approximately 66 per cent. For women the decline was even greater. Almost 80 per cent of women between the age of 55 to 64 live in a family household and by the age of 75 less than 35 per cent are still in the home. You can see that we have people who might be living at home but a good portion of them are not living at home and as a result of that they are in need of a support system such as the Canada Pension Plan.
While they might or might not be living at home, I do not want anyone to get the impression that after they reach the age of 65 they sit idle. You will be very happy to know that about 25 per cent of women over the age of 65 and over 20 per cent of men over the age of 55 do a tremendous amount of volunteer work in our communities for a variety of charitable and non-profit organizations. We are seeing an incredible trend in people who are retired from the work force. It seems that they are catching on fairly quickly in acknowledging the need for education. As a matter of fact presently there is in excess of 5,300 seniors enrolled in Canadian universities. Most of these seniors are enrolled in part time courses and they take advantage of programs that many universities have been offering senior citizens free of tuition, which is something they are to be commended for.
November 29, 1991

Also, full-time enrolment has increased by almost 70 per cent for undergraduate study and by over 40 per cent for graduate levels.
Not only is it a challenge we are going to face to ensure that we have enough funds in our budget to deal with issues such as pensions, we also have to be geared toward introducing programs that cater to the senior citizen population in the year 2011.
As a result of that, it requires an overhaul of all our existing systems to ensure that those systems are meeting the needs of our seniors, and not only our seniors of today but also the seniors of tomorrow.
The ideal plan would be one that you can use and apply without any difficulties and without any worry. Unfortunately the existing Canada Pension Plan, when it was introduced in 1966, was built around the limit of the 25 per cent figure in the hope that employees would have other plans, such as the occupational pension plans, the registered retirement plans, and some other revenues that seniors could bank on.
Unfortunately this expectation was not realistic because many of the people who are now receiving benefits did not rely on registered savings plans. The reason is that the registered savings plan is used by people who earn quite a bit of money, in excess of $35,000 or $40,000.
As a result of that the benefit of that particular plan was not available. While we invest in excess of about $7 billion a year in retirement benefits by over two million seniors, the simple fact is that many of those seniors have to go to other sources to guarantee that ends meet at the end of the month.
Let us look at some examples. If we are to look at the different programs and see what the maximum a senior citizen or a retired individual can collect from all of the possible pensions, we will find that a single person is relying on Canada Pension Plan benefits of around $6,800, old age pension of about $4,000, the guaranteed annual income in some cases of about $1,400 or $1,500, for a total income of about $12,200.
In an urban centre the poverty line is approximately $12,000 a year. Therefore, the system, even if it is used to the limit, barely deals with the problem.
Government Orders
To that extent, our pension plans, even though they are very fine plans, are still not really meeting the objective as one would like to see them doing.
For example, in 1989, 57 per cent of single people between the ages of 65 and 69 had an income below $15,000 a year, and 68 per cent of the people over the age of 70 had an income below $15,000. Those figures are only the tip of the iceberg. In the same year close to 40 per cent of all single senior citizens lived below the poverty line, as established by Statistics Canada. Approximately four out of every 10 senior citizens live below the poverty line.
Of single elderly people living below the poverty line, about 80 per cent of those people are women. About 41 per cent of all single females who live below the poverty line and 26.9 per cent of all males who live below the poverty line are asking for help or seeking assistance. This is a situation that needs to be addressed. However, if we are to just introduce a plan and not look at the cost of living or the different types of difficulties our seniors are faced with, in the very near future we will see a greater number of our seniors living below the poverty line. That will be a catastrophe.
While I indicated that there are a lot of good things in the proposed bill, there seem to be some difficulties. My colleague from Winnipeg North has stated his views on those issues. For instance, the current Pension Plan Act defines conditions necessary for receiving disability benefits as being severe and prolonged. This language, as it has been stated, is quite ambiguous. Our suggestion, made by my colleague, is that the definition of "severe" should be a person who is unable to do his or her usual type of work without mental or physical pain, preventing the person from fully discharging duties of that job as determined by a licensed medical doctor.
Unfortunately in my constituency office we are faced with a situation in which somebody who had a heart attack and applied for his pension had great difficulties trying to receive benefits. We also wanted to see "prolonged" defined as three months or more of continued disabilities.
There are other amendments that my colleague tried to put before the House. Unfortunately many of those amendments were not adopted. However I would like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that in the area of the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowance and the Old Age Security Act there is a need for a close

Government Orders
look at not only the over-all management of it but the services we are providing to the community.
You will be surprised to learn that in some cases for an applicant to receive benefits that applicant would have to wait in excess of about four months. There is a tremendous backlog of applicants, in excess of 50,000 across Canada. It takes about three months to get a slight change in address of an applicant or an existing potential beneficiary.
Those are issues the government should look at. In closing, I would like to say that I wish the government would look at our amendments as presented by my colleague from Winnipeg North and try to deal with them in an appropriate fashion.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure my hon. colleague from Ottawa Centre is aware that currently in the Canada Pension Plan Disability Benefits section, these benefits may be severed if the beneficiary tries to retrain for re-entry into the work force.
As critic for the disabled, I was working with the task force across Canada this past spring and summer. One of the comments that almost everybody who appeared before this task force mentioned was that these people are trapped because they are getting this disability pension. If they should try to stop being completely supported by the government and get retraining or get a minimum wage job they would immediately have all of these benefits cut off.
That means they have to try to get back on to these disability pensions, or they just do not make the move at all because they have no means of support. Without this disability pension they cannot pay for their equipment or the medicine that they need regularly and that they must pay for.
I just wondered if he agrees with me that it is too bad the government did not accept the amendment suggested by our colleague that would allow disabled Canada Pension Plan beneficiaries to take training or education courses in a recognized institution and prepare for alternate work without forfeiting the benefits
they were getting. This would be a very reasonable thing to have included in this bill.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the member for Hamilton Mountain for a question very well put.
I know she has been involved with the task force that travelled across the country to listen to the concerns of the disabled. She has done a magnificent job in this area. I am looking forward, as well as my colleagues and I am sure all members of this House, to receiving a copy of her final report so we can exchange some information in this area.
Certainly the member raised a very good question. Any system, any type of benefit or any type of program should never penalize the recipient if he or she is taking any type of training courses or achieving any type of education to further their knowledge or make them better citizens.
There is no question in my mind that when you look at the system that we have in place, whether the benefit that my colleague is talking about or any type of benefit, you can see that it does discriminate against people who want to become better citizens in our society.
For that reason, the government has a moral obligation to look at all of our social welfare and social assistance programs to ensure that those programs are not only meeting the needs and objectives they were created to meet, but also that they could be used as an incentive to encourage and help those recipients who decide to receive an education or go back to training institutions.
As my colleague indicated, right now it is the opposite. The system is in fact discriminating against those who want to improve their qualifications and become better citizens.
That takes me to another point. We seem all the time to be dealing with the problem rather than trying to anticipate problems or putting plans in place that would prevent problems from taking place.
It is my hope that we will shift away from the short-term proposals to long-term proposals that will change our society as a whole. I think the act is a good one. I think there is a lot of merit in it. However, examples like the one my colleague spoke of, which the government should look at very seriously, shows there is no need why they cannot amend or change it.
November 29, 1991

There is no reason why. I do not see why they do not look at those amendments and implement them. Someone might say: "It is a little too late". However, it is never too late. The bill has gone for third reading, and after the bill will be on its way to the Senate. Maybe the minister will meet with the officials of the Senate and try to introduce those amendments.
I want to close by congratulating my colleague on her great work in the area. It is a very well put question. I totally agree with her.

Madam Speaker, one of the problems we have had with the federal-provincial assistance plans over the years has been that every time someone on provincial assistance programs receives the Canada Pension Plan, their provincial moneys are reduced by the same amount as their Canada Pension Plan. Therefore, they are really no better off than they were before. They may indeed have a very serious medical problem.
I would just like to have the hon. member comment on this. In my offices we have settled case after case for Canada pension recipients. I must say that the Canada Pension Plan personnel have been very good to deal with as far as this member is concerned. I give them full marks because they do have a tremendous burden of work.
I would like the hon. member to comment on this process, because it seems to me that it does not solve a major problem for the individual when he starts receiving a cheque from the federal hand and ceases to get the same amount from the province. That really does not solve his or her problem. Would he comment on that, please?

Madam Speaker, that is a very well put question. This is another example that helps to make the case that what we have before us, while it does deal with part of the problem, does not seem to be able to deal with the problem as a whole.
To that extent, I hoped that the federal government would have had a chance to study our amendment and our suggestions so that loopholes in the system, such as the one my colleague has mentioned, could have been dealt with in a very equitable and forceful way.
There is no doubt in my mind that our seniors and people who are retiring should not be running around trying to go to this agency or that agency. They would not have to do all that if the system in place was fine-tuned and it was properly organized so that it was a one-stop shopping arrangement.
Government Orders
A senior citizen or retired person should not have to be fighting with this agency and that agency, this level of government and that level of government, and going from this account to that account. It is really quite frustrating and I can understand why the hon. member is raising this point.
I do not know when the government is going to sit down and have a look at the way we do things when it comes to providing services for our seniors. As I indicated a little earlier, the time has come for us to address the whole question of a society that has an aging population and a shrinking tax base, a society with a lot more to offer and a lot to lose unless we focus on issues of long-term planning for both our seniors and our youth.

Madam Speaker, as I see you in the chair today doing your usual fine job of chairing this House it reminds me that it was also a woman who initially introduced the Canada Pension Plan to this House.
The Canada Pension Plan was introduced in this House by the Hon. Judy LaMarsh and became effective on January 1,1966. Prior to that the Hon. Edgar Benson, who was then Minister of National Revenue, did the spade work with the provinces, going from province to province meeting with the ministers of health in order to put the plan together. Then the Hon. Judy LaMarsh introduced it and piloted the legislation through this House.
In her memory I think it is very important to state today that this legislation, which she piloted through the House back in the early 1960s, has been a tremendous service to tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of Canadians. We will salute her today.
The Canada Pension Plan is one of the great support blocks, the cornerstone in many ways, of our social net in this country. Many people come to my office who have been turned down when they applied for Canada pension, and we take up their case for them.
The first thing that I always insist on when talking to them is that they bring in the doctor's report. Sometimes doctors give them a report saying they are capable of doing light work. That is the worst thing that can happen to them because it does not say they are disabled. Of course in the particular area that I represent-and I know that many other members in this House are in the same position-there really is not that much light work for people to do. You are limiting them in their terms of employment. Also, they are not really well enough to go to work. They will take work if they can get it, and they

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
suffer while at work, but when they apply for Canada pension the bottom line is that they need a clear-cut statement from their doctor that they are in fact in need of Canada pension and are disabled in medical terms.
I want to commend the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare today for bringing in this bill. Naturally there are other things that I would have liked to have seen in it, such as those amendments brought forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, one of my colleagues who has done a very good job in playing the role of opposition critic for Health and Welfare Canada.
The minister has brought this bill forward in a manner that is going to help the Canada pension fund to continue. As a former chairman of the public accounts committee of this House, I am very pleased to note in the bill that the funds in the Canada Pension Plan will be scrutinized by the Auditor General of Canada to ensure that the fund is sound. Of course this bill today goes a long way toward making that fund sound.
The $42 billion in it today will pay for the demands on the fund for the next two years. That is a massive payroll going out there in two years' time. However, if the increased contributions that will be requested of Canadians and employers are not included and not put into the fund at this time, there will only be six months of necessary funds left in the over-all fund of the Canada Pension Plan.
This plan is of great benefit to Canadians. It really is a safety net for many people. In my view this plan and medicare are two things that really have to be scrutinized and kept in good financial shape so that Canadians today and in the future can look forward to medical plans.
In the United States in a recent election someone campaigned on having a medicare program and turned around a 45 per cent public opinion vote deficit into a big plus and was elected in a landslide. One can understand that, because Americans do not have the fine programs that we have, such as the Canada Pension Plan and medicare.
I think there is a good rapport in this House of Commons for working toward this.
By bringing in this bill today which will increase the contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, it will mean that for years to come those people who are working today will pay into it, that the fund will be there 20 years from now for them. If those rates had not been increased and if the plan were not kept in good financial condition, they would not be able to gain those funds. This is really an insurance plan for Canadians. Hopefully everyone benefits from it at one stage or another.
The extended benefits to families is a very important part of the Canada Pension Plan. As we look at the plan there is a need to increase the payments for widows or widowers left with small children today.
For example, people under 35 years of age who loses a spouse can get benefits if they have dependants. In today's world with the one-parent family having to pay additional costs for bringing up those children in a good and responsible way, people need this additional assistance. It is very important that this bill addresses that fact and that more money be placed in the hands of people when they are going through a traumatic part of their life, when they have lost their life partner and when they have children to raise strictly on their own. It is not an easy thing to face. However, it does give such individuals some hope and some encouragement when they realize that the Canada Pension Plan is there to help them out.
It is very important that this Parliament follow through on that great work introduced in this House by the Hon. Judy LaMarsh, since deceased, a great contribution to Canadian politics.
Under the current contributions the amount would diminish to six months by the year 2001.1 think I stated a while ago "in two years' time". If I did that is wrong. It should be that there would only be six months' benefits in the fund to pay out by the year 2001 instead of the present two years of $42 billion which are in there to pay for benefits.
November 29, 1991

It is very important that any of these funds be kept constant and in good shape. We hear a lot today about the non-viability of pension funds. We know that these funds are looked at by financial experts. If these plans are not viable then the contributions have to be increased. If we want these kinds of benefits to continue in Canada, which I am sure everyone does, then we will have to pay for them.
It does not come at an easy time because of the economy and because of people having lost their jobs. The only hope that we have is at least these people are paying into something that they or their families will benefit from eventually.
For the provision of increased benefits for the 170,000 children of deceased plan participants, benefit amounts will rise as of January 1992 to $148 per month from $113. Those are some of the trends about which I spoke that are very necessary.
Other people have gone into the details of this. I will not repeat them because it would only be repetition.
However, I do want to say that my colleague from Winnipeg North brought in some very good amendments to this legislation. I think that when he tackled the reasons for receiving disability benefits as being if a person was in severe physical condition or had a prolonged medical condition, the words "severe" and "prolonged" are pretty nebulous terms. How do we define them when it comes to deciding whether or not a person gets a pension?
We know that in the committee stage those two words were changed to "significant medical condition" or to "an extended medical handicap". Those two are sort of generalized terms and do not mean very much when we are trying to make a decision. He brought in an amendment of course to define that much better, along with several other amendments. I compliment him on that.
I want to say to the government that this bill is certainly due. I thank the government for bringing it in at this time. It is not very often in this House these days that we can get some legislation that really fits the Canadian mould and that we can come to a good sense of agreement on. While we in the Official Opposition had
Government Orders
some amendments to make and they were not adopted, I do not compliment the minister on that. I think the bottom line of this legislation is such that it makes the Canada Pension Plan viable today and right on into the future. That certainly should be the aim of every member in this House.
In conclusion, I want to say that a lot of people over the years have contributed very good ideas to the Canada Pension Plan. A lot of them have come from John Q public out there, people who come into our offices and make suggestions. I suppose they sometimes feel those ideas never get passed on or they are just talking to their member. I think it is important to note that in the committee stage some of those ideas did come out.
I know that I have certainly talked from time to time to various ministers about ideas that have been put forward.
I think that is very basic to any legislation in this House.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your patience. I hope after this legislation is in place that we will not stop there, that we will be looking forward to more timely amendments along the way. Perhaps some of the amendments that we proposed during the course of this debate will eventually get adopted.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few brief comments with respect to this piece of legislation.
The Canada Pension Plan is one of the most important pieces of legislation that we have in our statutes today. It is certainly a piece of legislation that is there as a result of the long-standing efforts of the New Democratic Party which has always been in the forefront of social welfare for Canadians, of pensions, and of looking after the average Canadian.
The amendments that have been brought in with respect to this bill are important amendments. They are certainly amendments that this caucus can support and that I can support. There are other aspects of this legislation that need some attention soon.
In my riding I have a number of constituents who have come to my office concerned about the permanent disability aspect of the Canada Pension Plan. The definition of permanent disability is an extremely rigid definition. It is unfortunate that many Canadians who I think all of us would agree deserve to receive such a pension

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
are simply not receiving one because the nature of it requires it to be permanent and longstanding.
I know there has been some discussion in this House about taking this matter back to committee to look at the ins and outs of this bill. I know there is a feeling on the part of a number of the members that the definition of the permanent disability aspect should be looked at to widen it and to include not only those who are permanently disabled but people who are disabled for a period of time and who may not be able to work for a period time and who are in a situation where they cannot work or are very limited in the work they can do.
As it stands now anyone who can do any type of work is prohibited from receiving a disability pension. That is an area that the New Democratic Party would like to see the minister and the health committee look at more closely.
The other aspect of the permanent disability part of the Canada Pension Plan has to do with time limits. To be eligible a person has to have worked two of the last three years or five of the last ten years.
Again I have situations in my own riding where people were injured ten years ago and only now do they realize they are permanently disabled and have made application. But because of the fact that they have not worked five years out of the last ten years, they are barred. That is unfair. There are situations where people who are disabled and unable to work have been trying to rehabilitate themselves and retrain themselves and have simply found that after an extended period of time and putting the effort into trying to make themselves gainfully employed again that it is simply impossible. They finally then turn to the Canada Pension Plan as a last resort only to find that the pension plan is no longer available to them.
That is unfair and that needs to be changed. It is unfortunate that was not addressed here.
I think the advantage of having the review of this bill and having this legislation before the House at this time is the fact that it has allowed members to highlight those points. I know there was a recommendation made by our health critic who indicated that he hoped there would be an extensive review of the Canada Pension Plan in committee so more recommendations would come forth.
I hope that happens because people in my riding would
appreciate a review of this legislation and would appreciate a more humanitarian approach to this legislation.
It is hoped that the Canada Pension Plan will stay in place as it is now and have the funds to afford to pay people who become deserving of the pension plan under all categories. Certainly the future of the fund and the contributions to the fund should be and need to be looked at very closely. Although there have been some changes there is still concern that in the future the Canada Pension Plan is going to be in some difficulty.
In closing, I would like to say that although this is a move in the right direction and is something we in the New Democratic caucus can support there is room for improvement, need for improvement and need for further discussion. Our caucus will be pushing very hard to have some of these items reviewed with the hope, the view and the desire that there will be further legislation introduced in this House to make the Canada Pension Plan a fairer and a more just plan for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the hon. member who has just addressed this particular bill.
I understand that there were a number of organizations that came forward to the committee and expressed concerns with the bill in specific areas that they had concerns with. speakeroldname: Mr. Robert D. Nault (Kenora - Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure this afternoon to enter into the debate on Bill C-39.
First of all I want to come at this from a somewhat different perspective. I want to deal with two major items in the time that I have. Before I do that, I want to just maybe outline to my constituents and to people who are watching what we are talking about here today, and that concerns the proposed changes to the Canada Pension Plan and its effect on our constituents.
It is well known to those of us in this place that the purpose of the changes to the Canada Pension Plan in essence is the intent to keep the plan on a sound
The major amendment is that the bill proposes an increase of $35 in benefits for dependent children of disabled and deceased contributors. This is a very admirable proposition. Obviously the main purpose-and it is well-known for those of us who are in committee dealing with C-39-is that in order for the position of this particular plan to be in a solvent situation, there have to be some increases in the premiums to Canadians simply because there was a miscalculation of just how many people would be paying into the plan. There was also a miscalculation of how many children, in the long term, in the 25 years of the program people would be having. Therefore, when they miscalculated, they had to revisit it every five years in order to put themselves back on a proper financial footing and back on track.
I say that just so people are aware that is the main reason why we are here today. Something else which is of importance to us all is there has to be some confirmation by the provinces that they approve of the amendments and the changes. That has also been done. The provinces unanimously have said that they approve of the changes to the plan and therefore everything is in place. After this bill has passed in this place, goes to the Senate, is approved and given Royal Assent the changes should be put in place by January 1, 1992.
One of the things in the committee that we dealt with was the difficulty that we are having with the plan as it is now. The issue of accessibility to CPP disability pensions was discussed at length. I want to tell you as a member of Parliament who deals with a lot of these issues on a day to day basis in my constituency it is a very frustrating issue to deal with in the sense that the definitions of the CPP have got to the point now where it does not reflect the realities of a modem Canada and of a modem world.
Because of those changes that are necessary to make this plan more accessible and make this plan more effective for all Canadians, we had hoped that during this process of the normal mandatory five-year review that they would also look at making those significant changes, for example in the definition of what is considered to be an appropriate definition of who is disabled and who is not.

Government Orders
The reason why I bring that to your attention today, Madam Speaker, is because we have on numerous occasions had difficulties in our constituencies with individuals who basically in a plan on the provincial side or in a private plan have had the ability to collect disability insurance. But on the Canadian side, which is the Canada disability plan, they do not meet the criteria in some instances. Therefore, it is not consistent with plans across the land.
It is very important for members of Parliament and very important for provincial members of provincial parliaments to try and put into place programs and planning that meet and go in the same direction. One of those areas is the fact that we do have the ability in the province of Ontario through workers' compensation to allow someone to collect a disability while at the same time go into rehabilitation or to indeed go into training while they are collecting. In our federal plan on the Canadian side of things, we do not have those abilities. So we are at loggerheads as to what our intent is and what our approach is and how we are trying to get some sort of training over a long period of time for the people that we consider to be disabled in this instance. They may have to go to a post-secondary institution and start all over again and take a four-year course. But during that process, they do not qualify to collect CPP because of the definition.
The definition of "disability" was discussed and mentioned at committee. I think it is important for us to read the definition. One of the first areas is what they classify as the two main tests under the CPP definition. One is "severe" and the other is "prolonged". Each test is taken separately based on the particular individual applicant.
A severe disability under CPP is defined as a disability which makes the person incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation. In essence that simply means in our plan in Canada that if someone wants to work somewhat part time, one day a week, sitting and watching as maybe a security guard at a department store, a very easy job as long as you do not have to chase the odd criminal, you could maybe do that as a disabled person or as someone who is incapacitated in a lot of other ways. That is something we should encourage.
We have to say to ourselves that we realize the amount of dollars we pay to disabled individuals are nowhere near enough to look after themselves in what is considered to be an appropriate manner. I think we should encourage people to go out and try to find part-time employment, even if it is one or two days a month, to get out and be active in the community and make a few dollars at the same time. I think we should encourage that. This definition severely restricts that.
The other part we thought we would discuss is prolonged. This means it is likely to be of long, continued and often indefinite duration or likely to result in death. Prolonged for me means any more than three or four months, six months or a year. That to me is prolonged in the sense of not being able to work. Because, as you well know, if you are not collecting any other forms of insurance you certainly cannot expect an individual to survive on no benefits at all for more than two or three months.
I think we should take a good look at that seriously to make sure we are not severely restricting those individuals who, as far as they are concerned at the moment they make their application, are incapable of doing the particular job they were doing and that somewhere down the line they will be able to improve on that. If we were serious about helping those who cannot help themselves in this land, we would make improvements to the definition as was mentioned by my colleague, the critic from our party, who has put in an amendment.
The first amendment basically suggests that we change the definition of severe and prolonged to significant and extended. Those substantial changes would give people the opportunity to make application in order that they can have some sort of income, because they are in essence disabled, and give them the opportunity to improve themselves somewhere down the line.
That brings me to the other issue that I think we missed the boat on in these amendments, and this is the opportunity under Bill C-39 to change the Canada Pension Plan. Bill C-39 should have dealt with something that we have been talking about in this House for many months. We are trying to focus the abilities of Canadians on retraining themselves. Under unemployment insurance we are now focusing more on UI, taking UI funds and putting them into training components in order for people to train themselves and to get accustomed to the fact that in a more global society it should
November 29, 1991

be accepted that they will have to be retrained two and three and four times in their lifetime.
On the one hand we are focusing on that regard with our training dollars under the Unemployment Insurance Act, but on the other hand we are suggesting to the disabled that if they have some sort of commitment in their own mind and do not want to continue to be on disability for the rest of their lives, they will not be able to take the opportunity and avail themselves of some sort of other education, some other training that will make them able to go back into the work force at a later date. That is completely contrary to what we talk about in this House.
In essence what we are suggesting to people is that once you get CPP then you better stay on it because the moment that you have any ambitions of trying to get off it and improve yourself, you will be removed from your benefits under this particular act. That is obviously the wrong message for the government to be sending.
In my constituency, as I said before, we deal with a lot of cases which are very frustrating in that applicants were not aware of the program, were not aware that they met the criteria of the program and were not aware that if they applied they would be eligible for CPP.
My colleague from Winnipeg North has put forward an amendment which would focus the government's attention on the fact that all Canadians should be aware of these kinds of programs. Simply because of the necessity of the credits that are involved in the CPP program, the longer they wait the more chance there is that they will not qualify. Therefore they will be left in a lot of cases, the senior population in this country, without any kind of benefits at all, without any kind of disability insurance.
I would think that the government and the communications networks in this country today could easily rectify that situation. That could be done very quickly. I would suggest to them that this is a good opportunity to send out the message to Canadians that we are open, above board and prepared to tell them exactly what these programs are, what the benefits are that they can receive. By doing so we would not run into the cases, as members of Parliament like myself and others are
Government Orders
running into, of those who come into our offices and find out that they have missed the deadline, that they no longer qualify because the period for application has lapsed. It is a tragedy when someone comes into our office. We know they qualify. They were not made aware of the program but there is nothing, absolutely nothing that can be done. I would suggest to members opposite that small change would go a long way to improving this particular program.
There is another change that some members in this place have considered to be of a positive nature. I am not quite sure that is the case at all. For example, they are suggesting that the one-year appeal process at the first stage of the appeal be reduced from one year to three months.
In most cases that I have dealt with in my constituency these individuals are not even aware because of the lack of documentation of whether they will be able to appeal. They are still in the process in most instances of trying to get rehabilitation under the Workers' Compensation Board. They are still in the process of dealing with the belief in their own minds that they can still work, that they can still be productive individuals. They want to continue to make the kind of living they were accustomed to before the difficulties which caused them to come to their members of Parliament to apply for CPP.
There is one positive aspect of changing the one year to the three months. At the same time it was suggested under the act and with the changes the government is proposing that they could write to the minister and the department and ask for an extension. What will take place now because of this change from one year to three months is that we will as a normal course as members of Parliament ask for an extension the moment the person walks in the door. It is an indefinite period as far as the act is concerned, with these changes. Now the individuals will be protected as they go through the process of trying to find whether they can be rehabilitated under WBC or whether they can be retrained to do something else under a training program from the province of Ontario.
In the meantime they will ask their members to focus on making sure they still have the ability to appeal the whole process down the line if so necessary.

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
I do not know if people consider changing the one year to 90 days as an improvement. The government has said in its documents and communiques that this will speed up the process. However, I doubt that very much. When people do know about the program, if they are fortunate enough to know, the only reason they do not apply right off the bat is because they are not sure they are disabled yet and are still waiting to go through the whole process with their doctors, their employers and with the WCB. Once they are sure that they have complied with all those requirements then they will apply.
There was a legitimate reason for the previous government to have the one year figure in there. As far as I am concerned, it made a lot of good sense.
I want to wrap up my remarks by saying to my constituents that in essence the $35 that we are giving in benefits to the dependent children of disabled and deceased contributors moves the cost up when all is said and done, with the increases that are to be forthcoming because of inflation, to roughly $144 to $150 a month. Not a lot of money but I think it is an improvement.
I want to say to the government that I am very pleased to see that it has recognized the importance of giving more dollars toward looking after our children. I am also very much in favour of putting this particular plan in its entirety on a good, strong, financial footing. I want to suggest to my constituents that we are quickly coming to the realization that there will be three workers paying for one disabled person in the years to come. That is going to necessitate a continual increase in the premiums Canadians will have to pay to keep this particular program running as smoothly as we believe it should, because of its necessity to those who cannot look after themselves.
The disabled and all those other Canadians who do not have their own pensions necessitates some sort of social security system. In order for us as parliamentarians and taxpayers to pay for these programs, we have to make some sense of how they work.
As I have suggested in this place before, when provincial programs reduce the amount they contribute to an individual, the moment the federal House increases the
amounts of dollars we are putting toward the individual's pension, it really resolves nothing.
We are asking in another amendment that has been put forward by my colleague from Winnipeg North that there be some sort of negotiated settlement between the provinces and the federal government to ensure that when, for example, we increase the $35 to dependent children the government of Ontario does not turn around and cut back a particular social program it has for those same children. That in essence leaves them getting exactly the same money before we stood up in this place and started debating this whole issue.
That is the sort of situation that frustrates many people and causes cynicism in this land with regard to politicians because it makes no sense at all.
I want to assure you that my constituents will be very well informed of this change, as I am accustomed to doing with all pieces of legislation that directly affect my constituents. I will let them know of the changes so that they will be able to make the appropriate changes in their own lives and will be able to better understand what all this means to them beginning January 1, 1992.
Be assured that we on this side are going to continue to look at the difficulties this plan has caused our constituents. It is because of them that we are standing here debating these changes. If we continue to get the kind of dialogue and openness that we have had from our constituents about the severe difficulties that are encountered when they try to deal with CPP, we will eventually come up with a program that will not leave people in the lurch, not leave people on the food bank lines. We will make sure that we look after our senior citizens and the disabled in this country in the way that we expected that we should look after them.
I appreciate the opportunity to make these comments today.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak this afternoon on this very important topic, the amendments to the Canada Pension Plan.
The Canada Pension Plan for me as a rural member of Parliament is probably, apart from unemployment insurance, the greater part of the workload of my constituency office. I would not say the more frustrating part of the
November 29, 1991

workload because no one can possibly match the mess caused by the immigration department, but that is a matter which we will discuss at some other time.
The Canada Pension Plan is something that does cause an enormous amount of activity in many constituency offices of members of Parliament, and more particularly in mine.
One of the most frustrating things that we deal with, as members, is the delays, particularly with Canada Pension Plan disability benefits. I think this is as good a time as any to put that on the record and to ensure that the ministers across the way, the large number of them listening to this important debate, will take note of it, as well as their parliamentary secretaries and other MPs who are listening.
For my part, I find it unacceptable that a constituent who would apply for Canada Pension Plan disability benefits must wait for months and months and months. Finally some eight or nine months later they will get a form letter informing him or her that the Canada Pension Plan benefits have been disallowed because the particular affliction is not severe and prolonged.
It is a form signed by some sort of a computer graphic affair that no one has seen and it takes the better part of a year to receive that refusal. Then the constituent appeals. They often visit the MP's office and we go through their initial application with them, when they have the initial application. This is another matter, as doctors fill those forms out and do not give a copy to their patients. If any doctors are out there listening, the biggest favour they can do for their patients is provide them with a copy of the application. Otherwise it has to be reconstructed in absentia.
In any case, several months later we try to discover where the application went wrong, many times of course without the benefit of the original application and without knowing what the doctor put in the bloody thing. How can one challenge what was said when one does not know what was said? Obviously one cannot do it very well.
Members ask the patient if they know what their doctor said and so on, refer them either back to the same doctor or to another doctor and say: "Get an updated medical opinion. Perhaps your situation has worsened since then" and so on. We get the second opinion, accompany it with a letter and send it off on behalf of the constituent. Then we wait. We wait six months, a year. Finally 18 months later the constituent gets a hearing. Of
Government Orders
course the hearing is always months after that too. Then they go through this second exercise and sometimes they fail again, sometimes they succeed. I see the minister sitting across the way listening to this speech. He was Minister of National Health and Welfare for a good period of time. I remember writing to him on numerous occasions about constituents who had waited for long periods of time and never were able to get benefits from the Canada Pension Plan system.
There are also those cases of people who fall between the cracks. I asked my staff to send me a few examples of such cases. Of course I am not going to name the individuals because I did not seek their permission ahead of time. However, I do have an individual whose case I appealed for her and eventually lost. This particular case involved a woman whose husband had become severely handicapped to such a point that the husband could no longer live at home.
To make a long story short, this particular gentleman eventually passed away. When his wife tried to collect the survivor's benefits from Canada Pension Plan, she was refused. The refusal was on the basis that they were not married. That should not have made any difference. They were living together common law, had two children who were teenagers, and she was the only spouse of that particular person. In other words, there was not a competing claim on behalf of anyone else or anything like that.
The good people at Canada Pension Plan said: "At the time of the death you were not living together". That might have been true but that was because they were not in a condition to live together. One person had become severely handicapped and could no longer live at home. They said: "Well we are sorry, but if you were not married and you were not living together at the time of the death, you therefore do not qualify for benefits". That is a silly argument.
I fought this case and I lost. I lost even though in this particular case the name of the husband and wife was on cheques coming from the same department for child benefits. The baby bonus cheques had the name of both partners. In other words, Health and Welfare Canada said with the right hand: "Yes, you are the parents of these children. Yes, we recognize both of you as being spouses for the purpose of administering the family unit insofar as the child benefits are concerned". However on the other hand: "No, when the husband dies you are not

Government Orders
spouses in terms of receiving Canada Pension Plan benefits".
How does that make sense? The rationale given to us when we lost the case was simply that the wording was different, the definition of spouse under one act is not necessarily the same definition of spouse under the other act.
Madam Speaker, I do not know about you, but when I go home at night my wife does not seek to determine under which particular act we are spouses and under which we are not. We usually consider ourselves to be the same regardless of which legislation we happen to be discussing.
That is one problem with this legislation that perhaps has not been discussed extensively. There needs to be a clarification of a lot of the language, particularly as it involves the administration of various programs under the same government department, not only under the same government but under the same government department.
I have another case which I would like to bring to the attention of the House. This particular person is a gentleman who was self-employed for many years and eventually became disabled and could no longer be employed in any way, shape or form. Canada Pension Plan examined his case and said: "Yes, you are disabled. Yes, your disability is severe. Yes, your disability is prolonged. No, you are not going to get a pension". When asked why he was not going to get a pension, the gentleman said: "Canada Pension Plan said I have not contributed five of the last ten years". We looked at the situation. We looked at the income tax returns of the gentleman and he had contributed in all those years.
But, do you know what happened, Madam Speaker? The last year that he worked he only worked about two weeks in that year. Because the contributions he made, and he did make them, to the Canada Pension Plan were less than a particular amount the income tax department had refunded them to him. It was totally beyond his control. He had contributed the requisite number of years. He was disabled, severe, prolonged and all that good stuff, and was still unable to collect the benefits even though he had qualified and made all the right contributions.
Why? It was because Revenue Canada has given him his contributions back. Did he ask Revenue Canada to give those contributions back? No. Did he know he got the contributions back 11 years prior? Obviously not, but he had and he was disqualified.
That is another case of a person falling between the cracks. I know. I lost that one as well and I defended him personally. Those are only a few cases of how people fall between the cracks of a system like that, a very complicated bureaucracy.
I say this to the government across the way. [Translation]
I am very glad that it has finally increased the benefits under the plan, but we should not pretend that raising these benefits solves all the problems, Madam Speaker, as our colleague from Winnipeg pointed out to us in several amendments he proposed. We should amend the bill some more. This does not mean that we in the Liberal Party are against the amendments presented by the government, but there must be more. I do not have to give a whole list; my colleague from Winnipeg has already done so. We would have liked the government to adopt many of the amendments we proposed. Unfortunately they did not, Madam Speaker, but I must still admit that the bill goes in the right direction.

I have a final concern about how the Canada Pension Plan works in its entirety. It is a worry I have and have had for some time as a former member of a legislative assembly of one of the provinces of this country, namely the province of Ontario. I cannot help but think that there is something not quite right when provinces can borrow money from the contributions of taxpayers for less than what the money is actually worth. In other words, they are borrowing that money at reduced interest rates to fund their provincial operations.
I see my colleague from Oshawa over here. He will remember our years in the legislature when we used to raise the issue there as well about how Canadians were contributing toward that plan. The provincial government would go into the plan, raid the coffers of it and borrow the money at subsidized rates and then never pay it back. There is a tremendous concern there. I would hope that members do raise that; perhaps not only in the context of this bill but otherwise. It is, as I say, something
November 29, 1991

that all of us in Parliament should think about very seriously.
If it was to be done over again, and I know this plan has been in existence for many years now, I wonder whether the wise thing to do would not have been to do something totally different. You could take those pools of funds within regions. You could not put this in one massive fund. There would be just too much money in it. It would be an amount that would be too large to be manageable. Within regions, perhaps provinces or even smaller units, we could have these pools of capital that could be invested in various businesses or other areas in order to yield a profit. That profit could be pooled together with the funds and then we could pay contributions to the people when of course they qualified to get them. I suppose that is water under the bridge. The system has been with us for some 25 years or so.
I come back to the concerns that I have expressed earlier. I want to indicate to the government that in addition to the amendments it has brought forward it should as well include either in this law or subsequent legislation amendments such at those that have been proposed by my colleague from Winnipeg. It also needs to co-ordinate the procedures within the department in order to shorten those delays which are totally unreasonable at the present moment.
We are talking in this bill about shortening the period of time that an individual has before he or she can launch an appeal. There is nothing in the bill that says that the government must respond within a certain number of days and if it does not there is a deemed benefit on the part of the individual. If the onus is applied to the individual taxpayer maybe the government should also be subject to it as well. That would light a fire under the chairs of whoever is responsible for some of these delays.
We need to ensure that we take all those pieces of legislation that have definitions or are outright silly or even different in the way that I have described with this one case about this woman who was the spouse of an individual. She had raised the family of this individual
Government Orders
who had been ill for most of the life of the children they had had together. But because he was living in an institution at the time of death they could not draw benefits because they were not living together and they were unmarried at the time that he died. These kinds of rules, particularly when the rules are different within the same department, have to be wrong. I could even say asinine. That is probably more the expression that comes to mind.

So, Madam Speaker, I too was pleased to take part in this debate this afternoon. With my colleagues, I again tell the government that it should have listened to the advice of the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who of course wanted to offer many amendments to improve this modification that the government has before us today.

Madam Speaker, I am honoured to rise in the House today to speak to Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act.
I come from a part of the country where the impact on every member of our community, on every family member, is very pervasive. It hits everyone in the community and in the family. This particular legislation is very important and touches the lives of many people.
It is most unfortunate that the amendments sought were defeated and were disallowed. This would have enhanced the legislation significantly and would have accommodated many of the concerns raised by witnesses who appeared before committees of the House of Commons. These witnesses came forward and put a human face to the problems that are experienced because legislation is regressive and perhaps not as helpful as it would be had these particular amendments gone forward. Motion No. 2 was disallowed. It asked that Bill C-39 be amended to strike down the deadline for the filing of applications irrespective of the mental capacity of the patient. It would have enhanced the lot of many individuals who have major concerns across this country.

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
We have to commend the members from Winnipeg North and Hamilton Mountain for their work on this legislation, as well as the government for this important bill. I want to address the bill from a slightly different direction, in my case as it affects seniors in the north, as it affects women in the north and the benefits to which they are entitled, as it affects the whole issue of poverty in the north and as it affects those northerners who are disabled.
The three most serious issues facing seniors in the Northwest Territories have to do with adequate housing, with the low fixed incomes and basically perhaps the abuse of elders. This is not by all individuals but it is a specific problem which I think needs attention and which is being expressed by that particular constituency.
The north faces many challenges today. One of the most serious is how we can ensure that our seniors in the north are taken care of at a time when the federal government is withdrawing financial commitments to its share of social and health programs. It is a fact that over the last week there has been publicity in the north that the government is withholding $50 million in transfer payments from the territorial government that would go toward health care programs. This has a direct impact on the elders, the people who are most vulnerable and need this assistance, and the people who would benefit greatly from the particular resources that are being withheld.
I have to say that I had the opportunity in the past to work with many of our senior citizens. In working with the senior citizens and with a group of other people at the grass roots level, I had an opportunity a number of years ago to work with 38 senior citizens and numerous others to help assist in putting down their stories about their lives. It is a real tribute to have worked with a couple of people, one by the name of Margaret Thom and another by the name of Tessa Macintosh, on elders in the north in a book called Nahecho Keh which we produced. It expresses all of the concerns that the elders have in terms of their lives and the struggles that they endure. We produced that book because we believed that our elders reflect through their infinite wisdom what values and principles are important for our survival in modern day society.
Housing is the number one issue facing seniors in the Northwest Territories. How does any kind of legislation relate to housing when you are on a fixed income and when you have a lot of encumbrances in terms of trying to achieve any gains you would make through getting your pension and you have all of these obstacles in front of you? One of the problems you would find difficulty with is if you do not have money for housing on fixed incomes. It is very expensive in the north. It should be noted that housing is also the number one health priority, a basic right taken for granted by most Canadians.
I am especially pleased to be talking about the issues related to health because it happens that people responsible for mental health are meeting in Ottawa to discuss this serious issue over the past week. Yesterday I met with our representative, Barbara Hood Hall, about the serious mental health problems in the north. Mental health is our number one health problem. As I mentioned earlier one of the causes of this illness like other illnesses in the north is poor housing. It is not unusual to have as many as 16 people living in a poorly ventilated, substandard home. The chronic housing shortage is a major obstacle to combating infectious diseases which plague many of our elders, particularly tuberculosis and respiratory infections.
A priority for the seniors in the north is the requirement for facilities in the communities with individual accommodations. There are some senior citizens homes in the north in communities like Fort McPherson, Aklavik, Inuvik, in the Mackenzie Delta region particularly, in Fort Rae, Fort Providence and Yellowknife.
There are 23 other communities where these facilities are still required, so housing and accommodation is definitely a problem for these senior citizens. Many seniors are living in public housing and are required to pay at least $150 rent, not including utilities.
The problem with this situation is that 85 per cent of the seniors in the north are on fixed incomes. The average fixed income for seniors in the north with old age security, the guaranteed income supplement and territorial supplement is only $850 a month. This monthly income is for residents living in communities where the cost of living is 30 to 60 per cent higher than the cost
November 29, 1991

of living in southern centres such as Edmonton, for instance. This means that the majority of senior citizens in Canada's north live below the poverty line.
For the most part, disabled people in the north who are affected by this bill, like the senior citizens in the north, face a greater risk of poverty than others because of unequal opportunities, discrimination, lack of recognition for the work they do, higher living costs and inadequate income support.
Many senior citizens are solely dependent on their pension plans and the money they get from their pensions through work because many of them share their moneys with the people who live in their family as a result of the extended family situation. They share their incomes with their sons and daughters, their grandchildren and other relatives. This is not an income to support one individual or two but, in a situation where there is high unemployment, to supplement the whole family's well-being.
The whole issue of poverty is another one that is felt because of the impact of this legislation not being so amended. The anti-poverty organization has identified one in four Canadians over 65 years of age as living below the poverty line. The risk of poverty is greater for women over 65 years who live alone or with non-relatives. Over 50 per cent of these women live in poverty, compared to 23.9 per cent of men. People who have contributed to the building of this country, who have put most of their life's work into building communities and sustaining families for the betterment of our community deserve much better than this. No one should have to live below the poverty line, but that is not the reality of our country.
I would also like to add that census figures show that while two out of five Canadians who had incomes in 1985 received less than $10,000 the percentage is much higher for northern Canadians, for disabled people, for aboriginal people including Metis and on-reserve Indians- almost 55 per cent.
Northerners, and particularly seniors, can testify that income is shared veiy unequally in Canada. In the 1990s our elders, our senior citizens, do not choose poverty. It is imposed on them. Similar to that of Canadian children who live in poverty, I personally believe that it is the most horrendous issue in Canada today. The homeless
Government Orders
and the hungry are a legacy of this country that we cannot afford when we have a reputation in the world of being one of the best countries to live in. The elders and the children of the poor are the most helpless victims in existence, and for me it is a national shame.
Not only are our elders victims of poverty but increasingly there is another problem. It is very difficult, controversial, and provocative to speak of it but more senior citizens are victims of abuse. I am talking about physical abuse, neglect, financial exploitation and psychological abuse. Our elders, our senior citizens, are being abused because they are vulnerable, primarily through their age. Elder abuse has probably taken place all through history but finally it is getting public attention. Like people who are disabled, seniors are abused because they have to depend on others to provide them with care. They are not only being abused by members of their family but they are susceptible to violence by neighbours, care givers, strangers and relatives. It is indeed a difficult subject to speak of. It is one that we would not believe but it is a fact that it exists. Statistics suggest that family violence, including that against elders, is more prevalent in aboriginal communities than in other communities. It is not a statistic that I, as an aboriginal person, like to quote but it is indeed a fact.
Knowing the issues facing seniors, disabled people and aboriginal Canadians, it is our utmost responsibility to provide the financial support for the programs and services that will benefit these important but vulnerable members of our society.
I want to conclude by paying tribute to all those care givers in the north, the employees or family members who are providing essential care for our senior citizens.
I would like to tell the members of the House that there are two seniors from Yellowknife who have given their entire life to look after others: those who are homeless, those who are poor and needed to get out of the cold. It is not desirable to be out and homeless in the north at 40 below. It is indeed a sad thing.
Ruth and Gordon Bailey opened their home in Yellowknife for years to strangers and friends who needed care. Now Mrs. Bailey is suffering from poor health and they have moved to another community, but they are still active in the church and community programs. If we were all as committed to enhancing the quality of life as

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
the Baileys have been, we would have a nicer and safer country.
It is incumbent upon us, as lawmakers, to ensure in whatever way we can that we create the best legislation for the people that need our help the most.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-39. I think it is a very important bill.
As we study and look at this bill we realize the significance of this bill, particularly that of the Canada Pension Plan and the other benefits we have in this country.
This is an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act, primarily with concern to increasing the contributions so that the fund will be sufficient. I think that we may lose sight of some of the things that really need to be done.
I want to thank my colleagues, the members for Hamilton Mountain and Winnipeg North, who have done a great deal of work on this. Not only have they done a lot of work but they are very compassionate people. Therefore, the work they have done has been very relevant. It reflects what we in this party want to get across with respect to the importance of this legislation and the importance that the people in this country are placing on this legislation.
Certainly the most important aspect today, as far as I am concerned, is the Canada Pension Plan disability. It is the one that Canadians seem to know the least about, mainly because if we are talking about the Canada Pension Plan it is generally well known that you receive it when you are 65, or if you qualify you can receive it at 60 with a reduced amount, there are also survivor's benefits and various other aspects of it. People are also familiar with the very important old age security and also with the augmentation and with the capital cost allowance.
I would say that the one that people know the least about is the Canada Pension Disability Program. That is because most Canadians have been blessed with good health. They have been able to carry out their employment without the necessity of having to worry about the
future, without the feeling that at some point soon they are going to have to cease work.
Of course, this does not take into consideration the ones that lose employment because they are laid off, because there are plant closures or because they are in areas of this country which are economically depressed. I am talking about the ones that have jobs they think will continue but because of health problems they are unable to continue their employment. This is a very tragic situation because I do not think, regardless of what anyone says, that a person wants to give up his or her employment. It is a very important part of not only their income and their every day schedule but of their dignity.
To be able to work and have gainful employment is a major factor in the profile and attitude of Canadians. When one has to give up this job, it is a very traumatic time.
I know because in my area the unemployment rate is approximately 35 per cent. The employment basically is heavy industrial. It is mainly coal mining and steel making. There are a lot of industrial accidents in which people are injured, sometimes at a very young age, and unable to carry on their employment.
Had this Canada Pension Disability Program not existed there would not be an income for them and their families. I do not know how my area would survive even to the extent it has at the present time.
I want to ask the government to try to imagine the ramifications of this program and the good that it does, to try to imagine the people who benefit from it and the regions of this country that are benefiting from it.
As well, I want to say to those that look at public servants as people who are uncaring and who disregard the needs of others that frankly the experience I have had with the public servants in the Pension Benefits Section, and particularly Canada Pension Disability, has been excellent. I found them to be a very caring, very efficient group of people.
When they are here in Ottawa, with jobs and good health, one would expect that there may be a tendency to forget those that are having health problems and are unable to work, that there would be a tendency to say: "Well, this person is not that badly hurt" or "That person is not that sick, I think they are really elaborating on the health difficulties that they have".
November 29, 1991

Although you may get some of that, most of their concerns are of a very caring nature. They are to be commended for the work they have done.
That being the case, what they are doing with this program is the best they can with the program as it now exists. There are problems with this program that frankly should be addressed. The member for Winnipeg North has mentioned a few of them. In fact, he and the member for Hamilton Mountain proposed certain amendments at report stage which were defeated.
That is unfortunate because I think those amendments were very worth-while amendments and could have added a lot to this program.
In one he mentions that in most cases, the standard procedure in turning down somebody for Canada pension disability is to say that their injury or sickness is not severe and prolonged. That is a very nebulous statement. As the members for Hamilton Mountain and Winnipeg North have asked: "How do you determine what is severe and what is prolonged?" It is extremely difficult to do because it is a subjective test determined by those that are judging the person.
If the person is in my riding, they are on Cape Breton Island and the people doing the judging are here in Ottawa and have not seen the person. Certainly, if the applicant is turned down in appeals and is turned down a second time, then on the third time around the applicant is examined by the doctor of the government, in which case the people here in Ottawa have a common denominator.
The problem then is that probably over a year has gone by and the applicant has no income with which to support himself or herself or his or her family. It really depends on this objective test. In that case I feel that the public servants here in Ottawa have been basically fair. I know that it is not entirely their determination because we do not have a definition of what is severe and prolonged. The problem now is that the tendency to say "severe" and "prolonged" is something that is going to actually be an incapacitation for an ever longer period of time, and that "severe" is a sickness or an injury which can be in some cases that the person is not able to move.
Along with the statement that the injury must be severe and prolonged one gets in one's rejection letter from the federal government the statement that this person is capable of doing light work. That is awfully
Government Orders
