difficult to take for some person who has a back problem who cannot even sit down and they cannot stand for long periods of time. To say that light work is going to be able to help or that they would be able to do light work is really not being fair to the applicant. I think this approach has got to be changed considerably.
Furthermore, in areas of high unemployment, where are you going to find any kind of work, let alone light work? As you know, Madam Speaker, in companies where there are jobs that are perhaps not too onerous, there are a lot of older workers who perhaps have a minor disability or a minor health problem who are given some of these jobs. For those who really have a major disability or a major health problem, there are no jobs. They cannot after they are 35 today go and apply for another job because they are considered to be too old. There are no jobs for them in other industries, that is if there are jobs that exist which in many parts of this country there are not.
I think that attitude about having to look at the person as being able to carry on light work is something which is very unfair. It puts the applicant in a position of feeling that the government feels that they are trying to put one over on them. I think that is unfair. It only adds to the mental problem that a person has when they come to grips with the fact that they have to apply for Canada pension disability.
Our party has defined what is severe as stating it is a person unable to do his or her usual type of job without mental or physical strain and preventing the person from fully discharging duties of that job as determined by a licensed medical doctor. We define "prolonged" as being three months or more of continued disability. I think these would be major improvements if they would be adopted by the government.
It would also downplay this belief that they could do a type of light work which in most cases they cannot, even if they could get the employment.
Suppose a person receives the Canada Pension Plan disability benefit. It may be after a year, it may be after two years if they have to go through two appeals and are examined by the doctor of the federal government. It may take two years. In this case they receive a cheque which goes back four months from the time they first applied. In the meantime they may not have had any income at all unless they were obtaining assistance from

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
welfare. That being the case, they are in a very difficult financial position.
I think there has to be some way of making it easier for the applicants to have some funding. I think this should be discussed with the provinces to allow for community services to perhaps be a little more lenient with these applicants while they are waiting.
It is not a risk to the federal government because if the person is successful in getting Canada pension disability, the province has a claim on the amount that they have paid in community benefits while the person was waiting. The province is reimbursed and the federal government does not have to pay any more. It does allow the applicant to have something in the meantime. This could be a long period of time without significant funding.
The other thing is that when the applicant is successful and is paid, of course the province is always there to make sure it gets its money back. If the federal government decides it wants to increase the amount it is going to pay the Canada pension disability recipients then the provinces decide that they are going to reduce what they are paying.
Consider the person who is on disability, is married, has children and the Canada pension disability is not going to be satisfactory to look after his needs. He is getting some assistance from the province but as the amount the federal government pays is increased, the province in turn reduces its assistance by the same amount. Therefore, the person cannot get ahead.
I would ask the federal government and the provinces to get together on this question so that when an increase is given the applicant gets the benefit of this increase.
I would also like to say that we must not forget families. Quite often when the applicant is on disability there are family members who are affected as well. Usually they are wives and children who must try to make do with the smaller amount the family will be receiving after the Canada pension disability locks in.
In the meantime there are the aspirations of the young people who want to attend university and to improve themselves. I do not think we can say that is not an important aspect. If we want our young people to be well trained and if the government is sincere about a higher
degree of education and preparedness for jobs in this country, then we have to look toward the sons and daughters of these recipients of Canada pension disability. We must make sure that these sons and daughters are not punished by the fact that their father or mother or sometimes even both through their diligent work and strong work ethic have become injured on the job. They find that their children are not able to receive sufficient education after that has occurred. I think there has to be some attention paid to that.
The plan says one has got to be able to do light work and that one can do light work. But it is not ready to allow the recipient to take further training or education to be able to upgrade himself or herself should the occasion allow it. This may happen even if it is an area in which they get this training and they can do this work without having to take Canada pension disability. If that is the case then the government is just defeating not only the purpose of the program and it is actually costing it more money, but it is taking away the opportunity of the individual.
I would hope that the government would look more favourably upon the recommendation of the members for Winnipeg North and Hamilton Mountain when they say that the applicant should be allowed to take training and to receive Canada pension disability until that training is finished and for a reasonable period thereafter to allow the recipient to be able to obtain employment. I think that is very reasonable and it would be helpful to all involved.
Canada pension disability may be the sole means of support for a family. Quite often when economic conditions become difficult it causes a great deal of stress on the marriage. Quite often there will be a marriage breakup, which is always very unfortunate. But wives do not know that they have rights and that they can be looked after. More and more women are realizing that they do not have to just be left penniless and that they can have some financial assistance. Unfortunately, under the Canada Pension Disability Program, their rights do not extend very far.
I would like to support what has already been recommended by this party in that the spouses on marriage breakup be able to be the beneficiaries of automatic splitting of the Canada pension disability benefits. That is if two people are separated or divorced, the wife has an
November 29, 1991

automatic right to a certain percentage of that Canada pension disability.
Quite often the wife does not know that she has that right and many months and perhaps even years may go by before she realizes that the right exists. I think it should be retroactive and there should be a conscious program to make sure these women have the right to the automatic splitting of the benefits and that they are made aware of the rights they do have.
If we are going to do that and we are going to be fair then this is something we should work toward.
I think we have to look at this as a program that is going to become more and more important. We have an unacceptably high unemployment rate today. We have a lot of people who have worked very hard all their lives in jobs that have been very stressful and injurious to their health and who have received very serious injuries. We have young people who are looking for jobs who cannot get employment. I think that we have to take a very realistic approach to those who have suffered injuries. Instead of having them go through hoops to prove they do have a disability which warrants this kind of assistance from the program, we should be more receptive to giving them assistance. If they are on the program and a job is made available, then that job is made available for a younger person who is maybe just recently married and has a family and a mortgage and needs a job very, very badly.
I think we have to look very compassionately at this program and what it can do for Canadians. I would hope that the government will not try to squeeze this program because this program is one of the few sources of income that low income Canadians have. It is one of the few means with which low income Canadians can maintain themselves and their dignity in these times of decreasing employment opportunities, cutbacks in spending on housing and reduced unemployment insurance pay periods. We have got to maintain the dignity of Canadians and the opportunity for Canadians to have an income.
This is a very important program. When a person goes through this kind of stress of losing their employment through injury or mental distress then that in itself is a problem. We should not at the same time ask them to
Government Orders
bend and to try to move heaven and earth to get the assistance under this program. I would hope that the government would be cognizant of what is going on out there and would be sympathetic and realize that this program is becoming, if it is not already, one of the most important social benefit programs that exists in our country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys and found his remarks to be rather appropriate indeed.
However, I wonder if I could make a few comments and then at the conclusion put a question to my colleague.
The member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys has served his constituency with great distinction for I think almost 13 years now. He is probably as well aware as those of us who represent constituencies in the various parts of this country. I am sure in that timeframe he has been made aware of numerous cases of individuals who have made application for Canada pension disability benefits and/or for Canada pension generally and that the timeframe which government has taken to process those claims has been inordinate. I am wondering if he has encountered the same kinds of cases that I have encountered. My constituency is geographically next to the hon. member's constituency. I find in my own riding that a number of applicants who are making these claims of the Government of Canada are having to wait in some instances three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen and eighteen months before there is a final adjudication as to whether or not there are any benefits which will be flowing the applicants. Thereafter the claimant has the appeal process, and that again will add another minimum of six months on his or her claim. I am wondering if the hon. member could respond to that question, whether or not he finds an inordinate amount of time in the processing of claimants.
Second, I am wondering, since the hon. member is the justice critic for the Liberal Party and a very able one at that, if he could perhaps give some consideration to whether or not due process is in fact being served when Canadians have to wait for such an inordinate amount of

Government Orders
time to get a decision, presumably and preferably a positive decision as opposed to a negative decision.
I am thinking, for instance, of the principles of natural justice. How in the name of God can the Government of Canada make an adjudication on a claimant from Hamilton, Ontario when the claimant is not before the officials in Ottawa who are making that particular claim? I am wondering if perhaps the hon. member could give some thought to that.
Finally, my comment and question, which will be my third question, is about a concern I have when the Government of Canada increases benefits, and we will say a disability claimant. Let us say they reside in his constituency of Cape Breton-The Sydneys or mine of Cape Breton-East Richmond. It has been the practice under the government of the former premier, Mr. Buchanan, and certainly under the practice and under the leadership of Don Cameron, the Premier of Nova Scotia, that when benefits are given from Ottawa they taketh away in Nova Scotia.
We in the Parliament of Canada provide a benefit to the recipient only to find at the end of the day when the cheque is mailed to the recipient the provincial government comes in with a big claw and takes it. The benefit which is bestowed upon the recipient is a mere fraction of a cent, thereby precluding the individual of that benefit.
As the hon. member will want to attest to, we are not talking here about large sums of money, but the money which is going to the recipient is indeed large. I gave an example yesterday-and I am sure the Chair has read Hansard and has followed the debate very carefully-of the $45 a month or the $36 a month which works out to in excess of $400 a year which can pay the fuel bill, which can pay for clothes for children, for milk and bread, the necessities of life.
I find it unbelievable and unreasonable that the Government of Canada is not making certain that provincial governments are allowing that benefit to go forward, thereby not precluding the recipients of the benefit in its totality. Second, they are not expediting those claims which everyone knows are taking an inordinate amount of time.
With your permission, Madam Speaker, I would like to hear some responses from the hon. member who has served in this Chamber, is a very distinguished justice critic for the Liberal Party of Canada, and has great experience as it relates to Canada pension and the
various claimants who have made claims under that particular piece of legislation.

Madam Speaker, I would also like to thank my colleague, the member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, for the questions that he has brought forward. They are very important questions indeed, questions with which he has been confronted in his role as member of Parliament in that constituency, which like my own is unfortunately a constituency with a higher rate of unemployment than either one of us would like.
I want to address again the third point he made, that is that the province takes away the increase which the federal government puts on Canada pension disability from any assistance it gives. The federal government has said that it is going to look into this and it has said in the past that it would look into it. Still the process continues. It is very deflating for families with Canada pension disability and the assistance from the province not to see that increase when prices have been going up and costs have been going up. How are they supposed to be able to make ends meet? We have been asking that for a considerable period of time, but it seems that the governments will not come together and deal with it. I think the federal government has to try harder to get the provinces to agree on allowing that augmentation of the benefits to go through.
Also as my colleague has said, and rightly so, this is an infringement on the rights of natural justice and the rights of an individual to be able to support his or her family in this day and age. What we are seeing, frankly, is a terrible tendency that government is accepting that it is right to have two levels of Canadians. If you are healthy and you have a job, great, you are going to be all right. You work and you pay taxes. If you are unemployed, if you are disabled and cannot work, then that is tough. You drew the short straw. We will make sure the roof does not fall in on your head or we will keep you in bare essentials, but that is all we are prepared to do.
I do not think that is right. None of these people asked to become disabled. None of these people asked to have these health problems. In most cases they have been soldiering on in the job for a good period of time with this discomfort and this disability, just absolutely reluctant to the nth degree to go on this kind of assistance because they feel that it is embarrassing for them. They feel that they are just not the same person if they cannot have a job. Of course they look upon the funding they are going to get which in practically all cases would be
November 29, 1991

well below what they would make when they were employed.
I want to go particularly to the first point the hon. member made respecting the process. I do not put a lot of blame on the public servants per se. I think it is the government that is really shortchanging the process in that if you apply for Canada pension disability it will tell you: "Don't expect to receive any word for four months". That is the starting point now. Four months is the time it takes for your file to get to the top. It evidently is a result of the fact that there are more people needed in dealing with this.
If you are unsuccessful you are told that perhaps your injuries are not prolonged or severe enough in nature, which is very subjective to say the least, and that you should try for light work that just does not exist in the hon. member's riding and in my riding. Then you go into an appeal process which will take probably another six months and, as my hon. friend said, it could take up to two years if you are turned down that second time before you go to the second appeal which would be the third level. At that point you are then told that you have to be examined by a doctor who would be a representative of the federal government.
In our area of Cape Breton the doctors that the people there have to visit are mostly in Halifax.
They have to get on a bus or a plane or get a drive and go to Halifax to be examined, at great inconvenience. They cannot go by train any more. That is gone. Perhaps in two years they are told whether their final request has been successful or not.
It is just not as good as it should be. The program is an excellent one, but the delivery is not efficient to the extent it should be. It is not in keeping with the dignity and the needs of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, one of the advantages-and there are many of course-of coming near the end of a long parliamentary debate is that you have an opportunity to listen to the words of your colleagues. We are often told that
Government Orders
Parliament is becoming irrelevant to the governing of Canada. I would argue strenuously with that assertion, having had the opportunity over the last several days to listen to the comments made by members of both sides of the House as they dealt with a very fundamental issue that everybody across this country regardless of what region you live in understands, and that is the need to have some sense of security as one gets into an older age and when one faces the sudden prospect of disability.
It has been for me a real learning experience listening to the experiences of constituents of Cape Breton, the constituents of the member from Saskatchewan. They were all talking about their kinds of difficulties and citing the problems faced by people in their own areas.
I only hope that this debate will be listened to. I only hope that we will understand this bill, which is what I call a fix-it bill, necessary to fix some clear problems that were appearing, particularly in the underfinancing of the Canada Pension Plan, has really through the dynamics of this debate generated a quite different perception and quite different understanding of what is going on.
If there is anything that should be taken from this debate, it is not so much the details of the particular bill or piece of legislation. It is that it has given an opportunity to open a window on the much broader range of anxieties and concerns about the level of the Canada Pension Plan.
It goes back to one fundamental issue. When the CPP was brought in there was a premise made, an assumption made, that there would be a much broader private coverage than in fact has occurred and that the CPP would almost be a supplementary benefit to the extensive network of private coverage. In fact the opposite has happened. We have not had the evolution of a broad based private pension plan system. There are pension plans there, but of course many of them are being eroded. As we go through this extended recession it happens even more frequently that pension benefits are being cut back and companies are moving.
I had a case in my riding just a few weeks ago. A gentleman lost his pension benefits because the company picked up its bags, moved south, and there was no obligation for it to continue paying benefits.

November 29, 1991
Government Orders
There is serious undermining going on in the private pension field, which puts even more serious responsibilities on the public sponsored pension system.
I simply want to use this opportunity to draw the attention of members and hopefully of the government or a future government to the fact that the reform of the pension plan system has to go beyond just tinkering, fixing some immediate problems. We may have to come to grips with a level of pension benefits that will be available as each generation of Canadians reaches retirement age.
I have between 18,000 and 20,000 constituents who make less than $25,000 a year. If we use today's calculations by the National Advisory Council on Welfare, their pension benefits plus their old age and the old age supplement would still put them below the poverty line. There is not sufficient build-up of a pension benefit to the CPP and the old age security to ensure that they can look forward to their retirement with some sense of security. That is particularly a problem in the larger cities like Winnipeg or Toronto or Vancouver where costs are so much higher.
I would suggest that the problem is that we should be projecting the profile of what our Canadian population will look like 10, 15, 20 years down the road and designing our CPP to meet that problem so that future legislators will not have to scramble to face a much broader problem of large scale insecurity because we at the present time did not exercise our responsibility of stewardship to make sure that there would be enough of a benefit base to satisfy those needs.
Similarly I find it also of concern that the number of real problems that have been identified in the implementation and administration of the Canada Pension Plan are not being fully addressed in this bill.
The member from Cape Breton who just spoke detailed very clearly problems of delay, problems of adjudication, problems of getting proper processing of pension benefits and in many cases being caught with all kinds of inconsistencies.
I will give an example from my own riding, if members will bear with me. I had a very strong and I think eloquent statement by Mr. Gerald Kelly. He pointed out that for reasons totally beyond his responsibility he had to take early retirement on a government employment
pension. He had a tax liability of $8,000 at the time of his retirement. No effort of his, of mine or anyone else's was able to get the government minister to move on it.
We are finding the situation where people are let go at their employment for reasons of cutbacks, stringencies and the belt tightening that is going on. They expect to get their benefits, but because of the nature of their pay-out they now must assume a lump sum payment. In the case of Mr. Kelly it was almost $8,000. It is an enormous penalty to have to pay, because of someone else's decision that you are no longer a useful member of the work force.
That is not fair. It is something that could have been fixed as part of this over-all pension area or maybe it could be included when we look at the question of Public Service pensions. The fact of the matter is there are people hurting out there as a result of the regulations and the administrative procedures that have been set up that penalize people like Mr. Kelly.
Let me give another case history of Mr. Carleton from Kenniston Boulevard who has been a member of the armed forces for many years. He discovered on remarriage after the death of his first spouse that survivor benefits were no longer made eligible for him. Once again a citizen who has been paying into the CPP honestly over the years finds out that his family no longer has the protection it has the right to expect. Again there were all kinds of representations, all kinds of pleas, all kinds of adjudication, and once again a stone wall with no ability to make any changes in that kind of case.
By the way, I received probably one of the longest letters on record from the President of the Treasury Board trying to explain his way out. What I find hard to accept is that we will go to so much effort to find a tortuous answer as opposed to solving the problem of that individual.
I found it interesting to listen to the comments of our House leader in this debate yesterday when he spoke at the beginning of third reading. He talked about the fact that many of these things are easy to fix, if there was a certain flexibility of mind, if we were prepared to take the administrative problems and just face up to them as opposed to defending them. As he said, it is no wonder people get discouraged about government sometimes

when they get caught in this kind of administrative sea wall and no one is prepared to give them a helping hand.
Another interesting case has just come to my attention. It concerns a gentleman who wants to make contributions to a United Kingdom retirement plan so he can draw on it when he is retired at the age of 65. However, he is not allowed to take any tax deductibility for it. As he properly points out, he will get the full benefit and will not be a burden to Canadian society if he is allowed to make those extra payments for the next 10 years or so. Again the Minister of Finance says: "There is nothing I can do about it". Of course there are things he can do about it. Tb use that as an excuse is simply not acceptable. There are many things he could do about it if he wanted to.
I have a file full of cases but I will just use three or four examples to point out that there is a real need, and the debate has shown this clearly, for a much broader pension reform in this country, to deal with the broad issue of the sufficiency of the pension benefit itself as our population becomes older. It is necessary to take a hard and clear look to tackle that problem in an effective way. At the same time but on a different level, it is equally as important to deal with all these twists and turns in which people get caught in dealing with their fundamental problems of security.
Therefore, we have to use this debate as the opportunity to make that case. I can think of perhaps no greater contribution this Parliament can make to the people of Canada than to give them a degree of assurance about their security.
A few nights ago I had dinner with an old acquaintance who is a senior ad executive. I was asking him questions about how his own business was being affected by the recession and by what is going on. He gave what I thought was an interesting answer and it is pertinent to this debate. He said: "The problem is that people are so insecure that they are not going to purchase, that they are not going to be making a commitment to the future when they know that in some capricious way they are going to be laid off, lose their job, be on the cut-off roll, find themselves with a benefit cut away".
Government Orders
I do not think members opposite realize what the cumulative effect of their eight year attack upon the social contracts of this country has really been. I do not think they fully comprehend the way in which it has changed people's perception of themselves and their role in society. We have spent a lot of years trying to build up a certain safety net, a social contract in which the fundamental psychology of security could be there so that people could become entrepreneurs, could become innovative, could take chances, could take risks, could invest, could feel that they have a real stake in this society. However, every time there is a claw-back, every time there is a cut-back, every time you niggle away at one or another of these benefits-transfer payments, children's benefits, family allowances-every time you attack it you are creating one more erosion in that sense of security, another sense of not knowing what the next day will bring.
That leads to a perception that makes people draw inward because they feel they have to protect themselves. That means that their best efforts and best energies are not used in an energetic contribution to Canada. That undermining of the Canadian sense that they are going to be looked after-not in a paternalistic sense, but that they have made a fair contribution and now they have a right to expect some benefit-has been, to my mind, one of the most damaging and eroding aspects of the last eight years. It is most always our seniors, who in many ways feel fundamentally betrayed.
It also demonstrates perhaps the most glaring problem that members on this side of the House have tried to bring to parliamentary and public attention over the last couple of months, and that is the condition of children. I listened in debate to the parliamentary secretary who talked in quite glowing terms about how this bill will add $35 a month to a dependent of someone on disability. She said how important that was but never recognized when she spoke that what she was really saying was what about all those other children in society who are not getting an extra $35 a month, who cannot get the $178 a month benefit, whose only support is the approximately $35 family allowance.
What struck me when the parliamentary secretary spoke on third reading and talked about this benefit for the dependants of those with disabilities was that she might have understood that she was talking about a problem that reaches out in a much broader way. One of the elements of security we have to begin to provide in this country is security for the family to provide a real

Government Orders
foundation, a real anchor so that families can feel they are part of it, that every time they reach a crisis, whether an accident, a marriage breakdown, a sickness, an illness, or a problem, they are not going to fall between the cracks and end up homeless, at the food bank, or without the kind of support they need. It happens every single day. They are not being supported any more.
I hope that changes in terms of dependants of those who can get disability benefits will be of some help. I still feel anguish for many of those who have not had the same kind of attention paid to their problems in any piece of legislation in this House.
As we end this third reading and this legislation goes on the books and we pass on to something else, I hope that we will not forget the lesson, that we will not forget how members of this House of all three parties who count stood up and talked about the problems and anxieties facing their own constituencies: seniors without proper pension benefits, people with disabilities, spouses who go through marriage breakdown and do not get a fair share of the credits.
We also recognize that those problems must be looked at through a prism and the light must shine on a much broader spectrum of Canadians. That is what this is all about. Security is not welfare. Security is not a handout. Security is not paternalism. It is the bedrock upon which we build our economy. It is the bedrock upon which we build a society that feels confident about itself and feels that it cares for one another. That is the way in which we are going to become a new productive society.
The government is out consulting with its new paper on competition and productivity. I have read those papers carefully. Unfortunately it does not mention what perhaps may be the most important ingredient in becoming a productive competitive society, and that is a society that feels secure about itself, that knows how to take care of those who are less fortunate and uses the full talents of all its people.
You will never become competitive and productive as long as you keep treating people, to use the words of my colleague, as second class citizens.
I support this bill because it moves to fix pension plan problems and toward those with disabilities. I hope to God that we will take this bill and realize that we have an awful lot more work to do.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every time I hear that my colleague from Winnipeg South Centre is participating in debate I try to get to the Chamber because if there is one individual in the House who has demonstrated an ability and a capacity to represent his constituents with vigour, enthusiasm and intelligence it has been the hon. member for Winnipeg South entre.
Not only has he been a very distinguished member of this House but he has served in other capacities as well in government and he has distinguished himself there.
He knows what he is talking about when he makes reference to some of the pitfalls of the Canada Pension Plan and when he draws to the attention of members of this House the inequities that are still within the system. I think he would concur with some of the very bright, articulate and enthusiastic members of the Public Service, but because of the restrictions of the law they lack the ability to rectify the errors.
The hon. member has made reference to the fact of flexibility in terms of resolving the difficulties. I think all members ought to concur with that. Flexibility is needed but what also is needed is some sense of discipline at the top when moneys are made available to worthy recipients as it will be in this particular case. In fact survivors will get an increase of roughly $35 for a total of about $420 a year. But we need flexibility in the Canada pension and we need discipline at the top.
You cannot ask a claimant to wait 12 months or two years or 18 months or 6 months before they get some sort of an answer. That is not flexibility. I am sure that the hon. member opposite who is a parliamentary secretary in his own right would want to stand and agree with me that that is gross negligence. It is not done by the public servants but by us, the lawmakers in Parliament.
I ask the hon. member if he senses any political will within the government to try to change these kinds of mistakes and errors. Has he sensed that? I have a tendency to believe whatever the response of the hon. member will be because of his distinguished track record in this House and because of the way he was represented


November 29, 1991

his constituents both in government as well as in opposition.
While the hon. member is on his feet I am wondering if he could respond to another question as it relates to Bill C-39 and the consequential effects of Bill C-39 in terms of pension reform. I will conclude with this question. I know there probably would be a disposition within the House for me to continue but I will conclude with this question.
The hon. member knows very well that this is a time of great crisis and the recession has not let go. Canadians from coast to coast, in Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan and the great province of Quebec, western Canada, Atlantic Canada and Ontario are feeling the crunch. Is it fair for governments to waver, sit on its hands and do very little if anything to assist claimants who are waiting in excess of 18 months in order to have their claims processed. I ask the hon. member: Is that fairness?

Mr. Speaker, let me first say to my distinguished colleague about his very complimentary opening remarks that if he does not go to heaven for the virtue of generosity he may end up in hell for the sin of exaggeration.
I would say to him that I feel inadequate to answer his question because I think we all recognize that there is no one in the House more knowledgeable about pension reform than our hon. House leader. In his previous capacity he was critic for national health and welfare. I hope the hon. member recognizes and that all members recognize what a contribution the House leader of the Liberal Party has made. He not only contributed to this debate but also to the whole momentum toward changing pension reform. He is still on the barricade demanding that we fight against the real problems that exist.
What I tried to say in my remarks is that the inadequacy of the legislation does not just stem from the broad brush strokes of policy. It also stems from, as he properly said, an attitude of mind at the ministerial level. Recognizing the urgency and imperative of the times we live in, there is nothing to prevent any minister from organizing special procedures for processing applications, for streamlining applications or for ensuring that there is quick deliberation. It is simply a matter of will.
Government Orders
It is simply a matter of saying how we are going to do it and using the best resources in the Public Service to provide a case in point. I can recall when I was responsible for immigration and we had the problem of illegals. We set up a special system of adjudication. Various kinds of applicants and groups could come in and we would process thousands within a period of six months. It was a good committee.
It seems to me that the same kind of answer could be found today. I concur. In this case I think a little bit of joshing is necessary. I find the same problem. When it comes to dealing with pension problems, people see it as some kind of Gordian knot that has to be untied. They see it as some kind of crystal palace where people have to walk through the maze to kind of get an answer and never really find their way out.
It is the most tortuous thing to have a file of correspondence this thick on one pension case. I think every member in the House knows it is the same problem, that we bum up more paper and more time and more energy on one case as opposed to having some minister saying: "Look, part of my job, never mind being a partisan advocate or a member of the cabinet, is to sit down on some Friday afternoon with my top officials and say that we have a problem and let's clean it up. Let's fix the mess and get the administration streamlined". That is all we have to do.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
